content: 1. Anaphylactic and anaphylactoid reactions, including shock and fatalities, have been reported with the use of cefixime. Prior to initiating therapy with Suprax, it is essential to thoroughly assess the patient’s history for any previous hypersensitivity reactions to cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs. 2. If Suprax is to be administered to patients with a known penicillin allergy, caution must be exercised due to the documented risk of cross-hypersensitivity among beta-lactam antibiotics, which may occur in up to 10% of patients with a history of penicillin allergy. 3. If an allergic reaction to Suprax occurs, the drug must be discontinued immediately. 4. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including Suprax. The severity of CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to life-threatening colitis. 5. Antibacterial therapy disrupts the normal flora of the colon, leading to an overgrowth of C. difficile. This bacterium produces toxins A and B, which contribute to the development of CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and could necessitate colectomy. 6. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use. A detailed medical history is crucial, as CDAD has been reported to occur even two months after the administration of antibacterial agents. 7. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic therapy not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate management should include fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, targeted antibiotic treatment for C. difficile, and surgical evaluation when clinically indicated. 8. The dosage of Suprax must be adjusted in patients with renal impairment, as well as in those undergoing continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) or hemodialysis (HD). Patients on dialysis should be closely monitored. 9. Cephalosporins, including Suprax, may be associated with a reduction in prothrombin activity. Patients at risk include those with renal or hepatic impairment, poor nutritional status, prolonged courses of antimicrobial therapy, or those stabilized on anticoagulant therapy. 10. Prothrombin time should be monitored in at-risk patients, and exogenous vitamin K should be administered as clinically indicated. 11. Prescribing Suprax in the absence of a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria.
